It is a right triangle: the vertical leg against the wall, the horizontal leg flat against the tread's underside reaching 140 mm out from the wall, and the hypotenuse running from that far point back down to the wall 160 mm below the tread. The gusset must touch the tread's underside along its whole top edge and must sit flat against the wall - it cannot float in front of the wall or cut into it.

Call the tread part `shelf` and the bracket part `gusset`. The panel thickness and the wall's position are in `globals.py`; read them through `hc`. Build both parts when the geometry is right.

prompt:
I want a cat step for the hallway wall - one of a run of climbing shelves, so this one has to be right before I cut the rest.

It is two pieces of the 18 mm ply we have in stock. The tread is a rectangle 300 mm wide (along X) and 200 mm deep (out from the wall), lying flat with its back edge against the wall and its underside level with the top of the bracket. Put the underside on z = 0 and keep the tread centred left-to-right on x = 0, so it spans z = 0 up to one panel thickness. The two front corners - the outer corners furthest from the wall - want rounding off with a 25 mm radius so the cat cannot catch a sharp corner coming down.

Under it goes a single triangular gusset, the same 18 mm ply, standing on edge and centred on x = 0. It is a right triangle: the vertical leg against the wall, the horizontal leg flat against the tread's underside reaching 140 mm out from the wall, and the hypotenuse running from that far point back down to the wall 160 mm below the tread. The gusset must touch the tread's underside along its whole top edge and must sit flat against the wall - it cannot float in front of the wall or cut into it.

The project already contains a `wall_plane` part: that is the wall itself, reference geometry for the acceptance checks. Leave it exactly as it is.

Call the tread part `shelf` and the bracket part `gusset`. The panel thickness and the wall's position are in `globals.py`; read them through `hc`. Build both parts when the geometry is right.

Tool-call budget: 52 calls for this task. The run is cancelled when the budget is spent, so spend calls on building the geometry correctly, not on re-verifying it: one final run_checks is enough confirmation, and build results already report bbox/volume/sealed. Stop and summarise as soon as the work is done and its checks pass.

Millimetres everywhere. Finish by stating the final dimensions you measured.

prompt:
Design a printed project box and its lid: two parts, `enclosure` and `lid`. It is going on an FDM printer, so nothing may be thinner than the process minimum wall of 1.6 mm. All the numbers below are in `globals.py` - read them through `hc` instead of repeating them.

`enclosure` is the box: an 80 x 60 mm footprint centred on the origin, 30 mm tall standing on z = 0, hollowed out from the top. The side walls are 2 mm thick and the floor is 2.5 mm thick, so the cavity is open at the top and runs from z = 2.5 up to the rim.

Inside it stand four screw bosses, one at each of x = +/-30, y = +/-20. Each boss is an 8 mm diameter column rising from the floor to z = 24, bored with a 3.2 mm pilot hole 15 mm deep down from the boss top. The bosses are free-standing - they do not touch the walls.

`lid` closes it: a 3 mm plate the size of the footprint that seats on the box's rim (so it spans z = 30 to 33), with a register lip 2 mm deep dropping into the cavity below it (z = 28 to 30). The lip is inset 0.2 mm from the cavity wall on every side so the lid drops in without a press fit. Four 3.4 mm clearance holes go straight through the lid on the same pattern as the bosses.

The project also contains `wall_gauge`, `boss_gauge`, `register_gauge` and `lid_go_gauge` - reference geometry the acceptance checks measure the walls, the bosses and the lid's fit against. Leave them exactly as they are.

Build both parts, and take a section view through the +Z midplane so the internal bosses are on record.

Tool-call budget: 38 calls for this task. The run is cancelled when the budget is spent, so spend calls on building the geometry correctly, not on re-verifying it: one final run_checks is enough confirmation, and build results already report bbox/volume/sealed. Stop and summarise as soon as the work is done and its checks pass.

Units are millimetres throughout. Verify your work with the tools before you finish, then summarise the result.
